**The Whispering Woods: A Tale of Forgotten Stories**

The first time I heard the whispers, I was ten years old. It was a Tuesday, the kind of day that stretches into the afternoon like a half-remembered dream. My father had taken me to the old oak grove behind our house, where the trees stood so tall their branches tangled in the sky like the fingers of a sleeping giant. The air smelled of damp earth and something sweet, like crushed berries. I had come to find the perfect spot to draw the story my teacher had assigned—*The Little Mermaid*—but instead, I found the whispers.

They came in bursts, like wind through the leaves, but they weren’t wind. They were voices, soft and overlapping, speaking in a language that wasn’t quite English. At first, I thought it was the wind again, but then I heard it clearly: *"You are not alone."*

I froze. My fingers hovered over my sketchbook, the pencil trembling. The whispers didn’t stop. They kept coming, in and out, like breath in a dark tunnel. I turned to my father, who was sharpening his knife, his back to me. He didn’t look up. "What’s wrong?" he asked.

I swallowed. "I heard voices."

His voice was steady, but his eyes flickered. "Voices?" he repeated. "In the woods?"

I nodded, my voice barely a whisper. "They’re saying I’m not alone."

My father exhaled slowly. "You’re imagining things. The wind, the rustling leaves—it’s just nature."

But the whispers didn’t stop. They grew louder, clearer. *"She is listening."* *"She is afraid."* *"Come with us."*

I ran home that night, my heart pounding. My mother was in the kitchen, stirring something in a pot. She looked up, her face pale. "What’s wrong?"

I told her everything. She listened in silence, her hands still moving over the pot. Then she said, "You should go to the doctor."

But the next morning, the whispers were back. And this time, they weren’t just in the woods. They followed me into the house. I heard them in the hallway, in the bathroom, even in the shower. *"You are not alone."* *"You were never alone."*

I started sleeping with the light on. I kept my door open. I even tried to block them out with music, but the words would slip through, seeping into my dreams. One night, I woke up to the sound of my own voice, whispering back. *"I’m here,"* I said, but the words didn’t come out right. They sounded like something else entirely.

Then came the changes.

I stopped drawing. I stopped talking to friends. I stopped eating. My mother found me in the garden one afternoon, sitting on the edge of a patch of grass, staring at the sky. She knelt beside me. "What’s wrong?"

I didn’t answer. I just looked at the clouds, which seemed to shift and change, like the whispers themselves.

One evening, my father came home early. He found me in the attic, sitting cross-legged on the floor, my sketchbook open in front of me. The pages were blank now, except for one drawing—a small, pale figure standing in the middle of the woods, surrounded by trees that weren’t quite trees. The figure had no face, just a smooth, featureless circle where a mouth should be. And in the center of the circle, written in looping, looping letters, was the same message I’d heard so many times: *"You are not alone."*

My father’s breath hitched. "What is this?"

I didn’t answer. I just looked at the drawing, and suddenly, I understood. The whispers weren’t voices. They were words. And the figure in the sketch was me.

---

The next day, I went to the doctor. She listened to my story, her eyes wide. "You’ve been experiencing auditory hallucinations," she said. "It’s likely stress-induced. But we should rule out anything more serious."

I didn’t ask what she meant by "anything more serious." I just nodded and left.

But the whispers didn’t stop. They followed me to the doctor’s office, to the waiting room, to the elevator. *"You are not alone."* *"You were never alone."*

I started seeing things too. Shadows moved when there were no shadows. My reflection in the mirror seemed to shift, like it was watching me. One night, I woke up to the sound of my own name being called from the hallway. I ran to the door, but when I opened it, there was no one there. Only the whisper: *"You are not alone."*

I tried to tell my mother, but she wouldn’t listen. She said I was imagining things, that I was just tired. But I wasn’t tired. I was hungry. And I was afraid.

One evening, I found a note on my pillow. It was written in the same looping script as the drawing in the attic. It said: *"Come with us."*

I didn’t know what it meant. But I knew I had to.

---

The journey began in the woods. The whispers led me there, guiding me through the trees, through the underbrush, through the dark. I followed them, my heart pounding, my breath coming in short gasps. The trees seemed to lean in, their branches forming a tunnel of shadows. And then, I saw it—a path. A narrow trail that wound through the heart of the woods, disappearing into the darkness.

I followed it, my feet sinking into the damp earth. The whispers grew louder, clearer. *"You are not alone."* *"You were never alone."* *"Come with us."*

I stopped. I couldn’t go any further. But the whispers didn’t stop. They kept coming, insistent, urgent. *"You have to come."*

I took a deep breath and stepped forward. The path led me to a clearing. And in the center of the clearing, standing in the middle of the trees, was the figure from my drawing. It was me. But it wasn’t me. It was something else entirely.

It had no face, just a smooth, featureless circle. But it had eyes. And it was smiling.

I stumbled back. The whispers stopped. The figure didn’t move. It just looked at me, and I knew, with a sudden, terrifying clarity, that it was not me. It was something else. Something that had been waiting for me all along.

And then, it spoke.

---

The words were not in any language I knew. They were not words at all. They were sounds, vibrations, a language of the heart. And they made me understand.

I had been here before. I had been lost in the woods before. I had been afraid before. And I had been alone before.

But I had never been truly alone. Because I had always been connected. Connected to something greater than myself. Connected to the whispers. Connected to the figure in the clearing.

And now, I understood. I understood that the whispers were not voices. They were memories. Memories of a time before time, before language, before the world as I knew it.

And the figure was not a figure at all. It was the world itself, the universe, the infinite. And it was calling me home.

---

I didn’t know what to do. I didn’t know how to go back. But I knew I had to. Because I was not alone. And I had to be with the world.

So I stepped forward. And the figure reached out, its smooth, featureless circle opening like a hand. And I let it take me.

---

When I woke up, I was in a different place. The air was clean, the sky bright. I was lying on a bed, and my mother was sitting beside me, her hand on my forehead. She looked worried. "What’s wrong?"

I smiled. "I’m okay."

She didn’t believe me. But she didn’t ask me to explain. She just held me, and I let her.

And then, I understood. The whispers were not voices. They were memories. And the figure in the woods was not a figure at all. It was the world itself, the universe, the infinite.

And I was not alone.

---

Years later, I still hear the whispers sometimes. But they are different now. They are not afraid. They are not urgent. They are just… there. Like the wind in the trees, like the sound of water in a stream.

And sometimes, I see the figure in the woods. But it is not a figure. It is just me, looking back at myself from the other side.

And I smile.

---

**The End.**
